How to play

Pick your teams, map and rules, then press Start. Watch lets the AI run both teams. Play puts you in control of one fighter.

From rank B, AI teammates can coordinate separate attack angles around a visible opponent. They check terrain and keep retreat, defense and relic duties first. The fighter readout shows an approach when one is available. In Play mode, Queued means a deliberate press is waiting briefly for a legal action; it does not guarantee a strike.

Controls

WASD or arrow keys to move. J to attack, K to use Force, Space or L to guard, Shift to dash. Tap an enemy to aim. With the battlefield focused, Tab cycles visible enemies; Shift+Tab moves focus back to the page. Touch controls are below the map. Watch mode has Previous and Next buttons and a team filter for inspecting living fighters. Relic carrier selects whoever currently carries it.

P pauses. Open the menu to change settings or start a new game. If your fighter dies, choose a living teammate or switch to watching. Pausing clears held buttons.

Command and deployment

Choose Command at setup to direct your AI team without controlling a fighter. Watch stays automatic. In Play, team orders guide your AI teammates while you keep control of your fighter. Use the order buttons by touch, mouse, or Tab and Enter. In Command only, A advances, S holds, D retreats, Space requests team Force, and F requests team guard. Play keeps its fighter controls.

Advance moves toward the objective and engages visible enemies. Hold defends the current cover bank. Flank stages on the upper side of the objective, then advances. Regroup gathers at a fixed point behind the squad. Retreat withdraws to home cover. The team readout shows the active order and progress; dashed markers show a reference point, or the assembly point for Regroup. The Flank reference is the public objective, not the upper staging destination. Arrival and timeout reports come from the active order. Movement orders are unavailable when there are no AI teammates. Defense and relic duties still take priority. Auto hands team decisions back to AI.

Each team can start in Standard, Forward, or Reserve deployment while keeping its Line, Wedge, or Spread formation. Deployment sets starting positions; formation sets spacing. Change either for the next round in the round report. Existing saved games use Standard when no deployment was recorded.

The round recap shows recorded kills, casualties, objective totals and a short timed event list. It states when earlier events are unavailable or omitted. It is a summary of recorded facts, not a complete replay or an explanation of why a team won.

Starting gear and rank

Set each team's starting rank, saber quality and Force type and quality before starting. The rank list includes SSS+ (entry), then SSS+ I through V. Starting high gives that rank's combat skill and bounded stats, but does not add past kills, wins or form records. Earned progress continues from there.

Rules

Control: reach 30 signal points or defeat the other team. At the time limit, signal points decide the winner, followed by survivors and remaining health.

Elimination: defeat the other team. There are no signal points. At the time limit, survivors decide the winner, then remaining health. An exact tie is a draw.

Relic: pick up the neutral relic at center and carry it to your home circle. Pickup is automatic when no enemy is nearby. Three deliveries win, or defeat the enemy team. Carriers move 28% slower and cannot dash. A defeated carrier drops the relic, with a brief pickup lock; either team can recover it. After a delivery it returns to center after two seconds. At the time limit: deliveries, survivors, then remaining health. AI fighters retrieve, escort and intercept.

Saber only: this optional modifier turns off Force attacks for both teams. It works with every rule mode. Sabers, guard, movement and dash remain available, except carrier dash in Relic.

Rounds can last 45, 90 or 150 seconds. Next round keeps the campaign going. Equipment can improve, worsen or change between rounds.

Teams

Line keeps the usual lanes. Wedge brings the middle forward. Spread widens the approach. Formations change where AI fighters move, without moving your controlled fighter for you.

Balanced targeting weighs distance and openings. Nearest picks the closest visible enemy. Weakest favors injured enemies without chasing across the whole map. Near the post favors enemies close to the capture point. In Elimination this is called Near center, and holding the middle earns no points. In Relic it is Near relic; carriers head home while teammates escort and enemies intercept.

Forms

Choose a form for each fighter before starting or between rounds. There are seven primary forms and nine choices because V and VII each have two variants. Each choice has six authored attacks; Ataru has eight, including grounded returns. Cuts sweep left and right, rise diagonally, descend or extend into depth with different costs, arcs, timing and pressure. Training helps fighters link the sequence. These are gameplay adaptations, not an official or exhaustive moveset.

I · Shii-Cho

Opening sweep, Crossing cut and Clearing circle use broad arcs and steady pressure.

II · Makashi

Measured thrust, Disengaging point and Duelist's riposte favor precise reach and economical attacks. Narrow strikes can miss a sidestep.

III · Soresu

Shelter circle, Close return and Patient riposte pair compact defense with shorter return cuts. Blocking still costs energy and can fail.

IV · Ataru

Vaulting cut, Corkscrew return and Somersault descent use real jumping arcs. Dashes become rotating vaults. Ground shadows, body height and blade contact use the same flight state. Landing costs recovery time; Force can still reach an airborne fighter.

V · Shien

Returning guard, Deflection sweep and Returning edge emphasize defensive turns and broad returning cuts. The labels do not promise automatic projectile reflection.

V · Djem So

Driving counter, Guard breaker and Descending finish trade expensive commitment for heavy pressure and counters.

VI · Niman

Converging weave, Balanced cross and Opening point leave room to link blade work and Force. Separate range, timing and energy rules apply to each action.

VII · Juyo

Relentless flurry, Broken rhythm and Fierce finish change attack tempo. Aggressive pressure has costly misses and recovery.

VII · Vaapad

Reversal spiral, Returning flurry and Controlled reversal reward defended openings. Vaapad is a distinct Mace-associated variant; it does not guarantee victory.

Fighting

Attack windups give the other fighter time to react. Hits, blocks and counters show the damage actually dealt. A block can still let some damage through. Missed, interrupted or blocked-off attacks deal no damage.

Saber attacks cost energy. Guarding and Force attacks do too. A successful block can open a faster counterattack. Range, walls, visibility and cooldowns still apply when you control a fighter.

Basic Force equipment keeps its Push, Burst or Pulse behavior. Training expands a situational repertoire: pull displaces a target toward the caster; barrier has a short duration and finite absorption; saber throw briefly delays blade use; grip and release requires a maintained connection; lightning drains energy; repulse affects a short radius; telekinetic sweep covers a forward arc. Windups, energy costs, range, sight and cooldowns constrain every cast. K and the Force command choose a ready ability for the situation. The panel shows unlocked abilities and the last action. Saber only disables the entire Force repertoire for both teams, including queued casts and lingering Force effects. Ataru movement remains available as an arena acrobatic action.

Jar’Kai and connected combat

Enable Jar’Kai separately for either team under Starting rank and gear. Two sabers sit alongside your chosen form. The lead blade and shorter offhand resolve separately, seven simulation ticks apart. The second contact has shorter reach, and either contact can be blocked, miss, or be interrupted. Two blades cost more energy and recovery; they do not guarantee an extra hit.

Watch the chambered pose, committed cut, contact flash and return to guard. Those phases follow actual simulation attacks. A flash at a target means resolved contact; empty air does not paint a hit. Offhand motion follows its queued contact. Form combinations flow from the preceding follow-through; the underlying attack costs and windows still apply.

In Play, the buttons show recovery and energy readiness, while the technique strip shows your next move and earned counter openings. A brief early J, K or dash tap waits up to eight simulation ticks for a legal action, then expires. It executes once. Pausing, changing fighters or opening the menu clears queued input. Move out of range, punish recovery, and save enough energy to guard.

What rank changes

Training improves reaction latency, reading visible movement, timed parries, recovery, combination length, energy efficiency and spacing. A parry needs a real guarded contact window; it is never guaranteed. Lower ranks can still win through openings, numbers, objectives and form matchups. The existing health ceiling is unchanged.

Terrain and weather

Walls block movement, sight and attacks. Low cover blocks movement and saber contact, but Force can cross it; nearby cover helps against attacks coming from its protected side. Rough ground slows movement. Marked vents cause damage.

Fog shortens sight range. Rain slows walking and dashing. Sandstorms have gusts that shorten sight further. You can see the whole field while watching; fighters only target what they can see.

Progress and saves

Team and fighter kills, deaths and assists add up across rounds. Career grades and equipment have separate limits. Form records show measured performance and give no extra stats. Round awards use recorded damage, blocks and objective time (holding the signal or carrying the relic); tied leaders share the award.

Save stores a checkpoint in this browser. Load opens it paused. New game starts a separate campaign; your checkpoint stays until you save over it. Clearing browser data can remove saves.

Version 1.0 preserves older checkpoints, adds team-level dual-saber choices, and treats older saves as single-saber games. Old attacks in progress keep their recorded payload. Continued play uses the new combat rules.

Older saves keep their recorded progress. New form records start from the upgrade, without adding guessed results from earlier rounds.

Lore and adaptations

Canon references support Yoda's extraordinary Force skill and duels, Force push and dark-side lightning and its defenses. The form tradition draws on both canon and Legends; Lucasfilm distinguishes those continuities. Lightning is offered to arena fighters by a sandbox rank rule; it is not a universal Jedi or Yoda ability. Barrier budgets, grip/release rules, radial repulse, sweep geometry, combos and unlock ranks are our gameplay abstractions. We do not claim a primary-source complete form moveset.

Further sources

This is a fan game. Form names and broad styles draw on this seven-form overview, licensed Shien artwork and Fantasy Flight's Juyo preview. The stats, animation moves and Force abilities here are game rules, not an official moveset.

Single sabers and Jar’Kai dual sabers are selectable. The short offhand draws broad inspiration from Ahsoka’s complementary shoto blade; double-bladed sabers remain a different weapon and are not selectable. The Jar’Kai name is also used for paired lightsabers in Atomic Mass Games’ licensed Ahsoka preview. Our dual-saber costs, timing and form combinations are original arena rules.

Animation research

Specific fight references include JamesKane2008’s Lightsaber Fight 1, whose author describes a stickman Star Wars duel, and thorax91’s Star Wars LightsaberFight, described by its creator as frame-by-frame animation. The pages exposed author notes and a legacy-player requirement, not verified playback. Our design takeaway is to author clear linked poses and synchronize effects with contact, using original procedural assets.

We consulted Alan Becker’s official stick-figure key-pose tutorial and animation-principles series descriptions for key poses, easing, anticipation and follow-through. The official Reactor Core Duel page provides a multi-opponent battle reference. These were page and description reviews; video playback was not verified. Poses, trails and assets here are original, not copied choreography.
